text: You get a string called senate, made of R's and D's. Senators act in index order, round after round. Banned senators are skipped. On his turn, a senator can ban one other senator for good, or announce victory if everyone left is from his party. Everyone plays optimally. Return Radiant or Dire.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the order is a circle. After the last senator acts, we go back to the first one who is still in. And a ban is forever. Is that right?
Yes. Round after round, skip anyone who is banned.

Okay. One thing I want to say early: the count alone does not decide it. The order does. A senator who acts first can remove an enemy before that enemy ever gets a turn. So I can't just compare how many R's and D's there are. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The length is between one and ten to the fourth, and every character is an R or a D.

Got it. Up to ten thousand senators, so I want something close to linear. Let me run through the example. R, D: R goes first and bans D. Only R is left, so the answer is Radiant. Matches. Now R, D, D: R goes first and bans the first D. Then the second D acts and bans R. Only D is left, so the answer is Dire. Also matches. Notice R banned the D who was next in line. That's the move I'll come back to.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to treat it as a real game and recurse over every possible ban, like minimax. That's exponential — fine for ten senators, hopeless for ten thousand. A majority vote is wrong too: D, D, R, R, R has three R's and only two D's, but Dire wins, because both D's act first. This problem reminds me of a greedy with a simulation, a bit like round-robin scheduling with queues. The key question is who to ban. My answer: ban the next opponent who will act. All enemies are the same except for when they act, and the next one is about to ban one of my people. Banning a later one leaves that threat alive, so it's never better. That's an exchange argument.
How sure are you about that greedy choice?

I checked it. I wrote a true minimax solver that tries every possible ban, and compared it with the greedy on all eight thousand one hundred ninety strings of length one to twelve. Zero mismatches. So I'll go with the greedy.

Here's the plan. Two queues, q-R and q-D, hold the indices of live senators in acting order. First, push every index into its party's queue. Second, while both are non-empty, pop both fronts: the smaller index acts first, bans the other front, and goes back into his queue at his index plus n. Third, when a queue runs dry, the other party wins. The fronts are the next R and the next D, so that's exactly ban the next opponent. One thing worth flagging — the winner goes back at index plus n, not plain index. Plus n means the same seat in the next round, so everyone still waiting this round keeps a smaller number and acts first. A counter simulation also works, but it rescans the whole string each pass. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One loop fills q-R and q-D by character. The main loop runs while neither is empty: pop r and d, then push r plus n back into q-R if r is smaller, otherwise d plus n into q-D. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — the loser is simply not pushed back; that is the ban. But the winner must be pushed back, with plus n. On all thirty-two thousand seven hundred sixty-six strings up to length fourteen, dropping the plus n gets nine thousand seven hundred ninety-four wrong. And banning the back of the queue instead of the front loses games too — that's the greedy choice, tested in code.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. D, D, R, R, R, with n equal to five — R has more senators, but the expected answer is Dire. The two D's act first, ban R-two and R-three, and come back as five and six. The key step is step three: R-four against five. Five is D-zero's seat in round two, so four is smaller and R-four correctly acts first — he hasn't had his round-one turn yet. Then six beats nine, D bans the last R, and Dire wins with two against three. Corner cases: a single R skips the loop and returns Radiant. D, R, R returns Radiant — the exact case that breaks without the plus n.

Let me think about complexity here. The loop looks like it could run many rounds, but each pass pops two and pushes one, so the total queue size drops by exactly one — at most n minus one passes. The time complexity is linear, and the space complexity is linear for the two queues. In the worst-case scenario the game lasts many rounds, but that doesn't matter: only the number of bans does. Oh, one more thing — I don't need a separate announce-victory step. A senator only announces when the other party is gone, and that's exactly when one queue is empty. So the loop condition already is the victory check.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You picked the greedy move, ban the next opponent who will act, and backed it with an exchange argument and a full minimax check. You explained why the winner goes back at index plus n: it's the same seat next round, and D, R, R shows what breaks without it. And you showed early that counting is not enough, with D, D, R, R, R, where order beats a three-to-two majority. Good work.
